name: Sheitel

lead: A sheitel is a wig or half-wig worn by many married Orthodox Jewish women to meet the requirement to cover their hair in front of men other than close relatives. Besides modesty, it provides a styled head of hair.
Styles range from traditional elastic-cap wigs with bangs to modern lace-front pieces and falls worn under a hat. Some are made of real hair, others synthetic.

paras: Women choose a cap-style wig, lace-front or fall, often styled by a specialist, and wear it daily. Many wigs carry a kosher certification (hechsher) about the hair source.
No specific health risks are described here. Debates concern rabbinic acceptance and the origin of hair; a 2004 ruling on Indian hair led some women to burn their wigs.

angle.text: A sheitel replaces the visible hair with a styled wig, in cap, lace-front or fall form, so the wearer presents a groomed hairstyle.[1]

lead: A sheitel (Yiddish) is a wig or half-wig worn by some married Orthodox Jewish women to cover their hair.[1] It gives the wearer a styled, groomed head of hair in public while meeting the religious requirement.[1]

Halakha requires married women to cover most or all of their hair around men outside close family.[1] Sheitels began to be used as coverings in the 18th century and traditional rabbis opposed them; Moshe Feinstein permitted them, and the Lubavitcher Rebbe encouraged them though he wrote a scarf would be better.[1] Many Sephardi authorities forbid wigs, and those women wear scarves or hats.[1]

paras: Traditional sheitels use an elastic cap, often with heavy bangs; lace-front styles give a more natural hairline, and a fall is a half-wig worn with a hat or headband.[1] The shpitzel, a front-only partial wig under a pillbox hat, was popular among 19th-century Hungarian Hasidim.[1]

In 2004 Rabbi Elyashiv ruled against Indian hair because it came from a Hindu temple tonsure ritual; women in Brooklyn burned wigs.[1] Wigmakers then began sourcing hair from Cambodia.[1] Critics debate whether very attractive wigs undermine modesty.[1]

timeline.event: Ruling against Indian hair in wigs.[1]
